messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
We prove the equivalence in two directions.

What does completeness give for the nested closed sets?

If M is complete and F_n are nonempty closed with F_{n+1} \subset F_n and diam F_n \to 0, we choose x_n \in F_n; then (x_n) is Cauchy because d(x_m,x_n) \le diam F_N whenever m,n \ge N.

Completeness gives a point x, and closedness of each F_k gives x \in F_k for every k, so \bigcap_n F_n is nonempty.

Does that establish the forward implication?

For the converse, we assume every such nested family has a nonempty intersection, we let (x_n) be an arbitrary Cauchy sequence, and we define F_n to be the closure of \{x_k : k \ge n\}.

The tail diameters tend to zero, and closure does not increase diameter, so the sets F_n are nonempty closed, nested, and have diameters tending to zero; the assumed property then gives a point x in \bigcap_n F_n.

For every n, x lies in the closure of \{x_k : k \ge n\}, and the vanishing tail diameters force x_n \to x, so M is complete.

Is the equivalence now fully proved?

What does completeness give for the nested closed sets?

If M is complete and F_n are nonempty closed with F_{n+1} \subset F_n and diam F_n \to 0, we choose x_n \in F_n; then (x_n) is Cauchy because d(x_m,x_n) \le diam F_N whenever m,n \ge N.

Completeness gives a point x, and closedness of each F_k gives x \in F_k for every k, so \bigcap_n F_n is nonempty.

Does that establish the forward implication?

For the converse, we assume every such nested family has a nonempty intersection, we let (x_n) be an arbitrary Cauchy sequence, and we define F_n to be the closure of \{x_k : k \ge n\}.

The tail diameters tend to zero, and closure does not increase diameter, so the sets F_n are nonempty closed, nested, and have diameters tending to zero; the assumed property then gives a point x in \bigcap_n F_n.

For every n, x lies in the closure of \{x_k : k \ge n\}, and the vanishing tail diameters force x_n \to x, so M is complete.
